name: Sulfur
toxicityNote: Flammable and can release irritating sulfur dioxide if heated; keep away from heat, children and pets, wash hands after handling and do not make elixirs.
physical: Traditionally linked to vitality and warmth
Associated with a lively, energized feeling
Admired by many as a symbol of renewed strength
summary: Sulfur forms brilliant yellow crystals around volcanic vents, and crystal lore links this fiery native element to courage, vitality and transformation.
intro: Sulfur is one of the most vivid minerals on the planet, a pure native element that crystallizes in bright lemon yellow, honey and sometimes amber-orange. The best specimens are sharp, glassy bipyramids that catch the light with a resinous shine. It forms around volcanic fumaroles and hot springs, and in sedimentary deposits with gypsum and celestine. It is extremely soft, brittle and a poor conductor of heat, so a warm hand can make a crystal crackle. It smells faintly of matches only when it is scratched or burned, and well-kept specimens are almost odorless. People love sulfur for the sheer color, which looks like captured sunlight.
history: Sulfur has been known since antiquity as brimstone, literally the burning stone. Ancient Greeks and Romans burned it to fumigate homes, and it appears in the Bible and in Homer as a purifying agent. Sicily was the world's main source for centuries, with famed mines near Agrigento and Caltanissetta yielding spectacular crystals. Medieval alchemists considered sulfur one of the three primary principles of matter, alongside mercury and salt, the principle of combustibility. Today the Ijen volcano in Indonesia is famous for its glowing blue sulfur flames and for workers who carry baskets of yellow sulfur down the mountainside.
meaning: Within crystal tradition, sulfur is a fire stone. Its warm yellow and its volcanic birth are read as raw vitality, will and the courage to begin something new. Healers connect it to the solar plexus and root, using it to symbolize burning away what is stagnant. It appears in purification rituals as a symbol rather than a tool, and many people prefer to keep it as a specimen that reminds them of transformation. It is said to help when motivation is low or when a person needs to find the nerve to act. Traditionally it is also associated with warmth, a lively feeling and renewed energy, particularly during the long, cold parts of the year.
howToUse: Because sulfur is fragile and best handled sparingly, display it rather than carry it. Set a specimen in a sealed glass case or box on a shelf in the south of your home, the traditional fire direction, or on a desk where you need drive. Look at it during a morning intention session and picture the volcanic heat that created it. Never burn it and never place it near candles, heaters or matches. If you work with a pendulum or divination, a closed display can serve as a focus. Wash your hands after touching raw sulfur, and keep it out of reach of pets and children.
care: Sulfur is very soft and sensitive to heat, which can crack it from the thermal shock of a warm hand. Avoid water soaks and long sunlight, which can dull the surface. Dust it gently with a dry soft brush, and cleanse it with sound, moonlight or by placing it near clear quartz. Keep it in a closed box away from heat, flames and sources of sparks. Store it by itself, since sulfur fumes can tarnish silver and copper, and wash your hands after handling it. Do not use it in any water-based elixir.
identify: Natural sulfur is bright yellow, soft enough to scratch with a fingernail, and has a resinous luster. It burns with a blue flame and sharp odor, but you should never test it that way at home. Look-alikes include yellow calcite, orpiment and plain dyed minerals; calcite is harder and fizzes in acid, while orpiment is toxic arsenic. Reputable sellers will name the locality, such as Sicily or Bolivia. Specimens that look too perfect or smell strongly are suspect.

faq.q: What is sulfur crystal used for?
faq.a: Crystal lovers use sulfur as a symbol of fire, courage and transformation. It is kept as a display specimen to inspire motivation and a fresh start, rather than handled often, since it is soft and flammable.

faq.q: Is sulfur safe to keep at home?
faq.a: Yes, as a display specimen kept dry, away from heat and flames, and out of reach of children and pets. It is flammable and can release irritating fumes if heated, so wash your hands after handling and never burn it.

faq.q: Why does sulfur crack in my hand?
faq.a: Sulfur is a poor conductor of heat, so the warmth of your hand expands the outer layer faster than the interior, causing tiny cracks and a crackling sound. Handle it briefly, with cool hands, or use a soft cloth.
